text:
My cradle stood beside the library,
a somber Babel where novel, science, fable—
everything, Greek dust or Latin ash—
mingled. I was tall as a folio.
Two voices spoke to me. One, insidious and firm:
“The Earth is a cake brimming with sweetness;
I can—and your pleasure will never end!—
forge you an appetite of equal vastness.”
And the other: “Come! O come travel through dreams,
far from the possible and the known.”
And this one sang like wind across the sands,
a phantom risen from no one knows where,
caressing the ear even as it frightens it.
I answered you: “Yes! Sweet voice!” From that moment
dates what may be called my wound
and my fate. Behind the panels
of immense existence, in the blackest abyss,
I see distinctly the strangest worlds,
and, an ecstatic victim of my clairvoyance,
I drag after me snakes that bite my heels.

And since that moment, like the prophets,
with immense tenderness I love the sea and desert;
I smile at funerals and sob at feasts,
and find a pleasant savor in the sourest wine;
facts sometimes seem lies to me,
and looking at the sky I fall into deep pits.
But the voice consoles me, saying: “The dreams
of madmen are more beautiful than those of the wise.”

translation.title: The Voice
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The source’s minor ‘de que parte’ typo is read in context as ‘de qué parte.’
